strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation leveraging recent insights (Stanczuk et al. 2024, Ventura et al. 2025) about score function Jacobians capturing manifold structure
Mathematically sound Riemannian metric construction with multiple interpretations (manifold-aware geodesics, pullback metrics through score space)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse tasks (2D synthetic, image interpolation, video frame interpolation) with multiple metrics and datasets
Consistent improvements across FID, PPL, PDV, and RE metrics on all evaluated datasets
Requires no architectural modifications or additional training on pre-trained diffusion models
Thorough ablation studies and analysis of design choices (timestep selection, spectral gaps) with clear visualizations
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations and theoretical assumptions
Good reproducibility: code provided, detailed experimental setup, publicly available datasets
weaknesses: Incremental improvements over the most similar baseline (GeodesicDiffusion): ~3% on FID, ~5% on PPL—gains are consistent but modest given added computational overhead

Significant computational cost requiring 500 Adam iterations per interpolation path; no runtime comparisons provided; much more expensive than closed-form LERP/SLERP alternatives, limiting practical applicability
Limited scope: primary contribution restricted to interpolation; extensions to other metric-related tasks (clustering, etc.) deferred to future work, narrowing potential impact
Theoretical contributions are straightforward: Proposition 1 is intuitive once stated; using J^T J for metrics is conventional; novelty lies mainly in application context

Small experimental scale: only 50 image pairs per dataset; semantic similarity constraint (LPIPS < 0.6) excludes harder cases; critically, no human perceptual evaluation studies—all metrics are automatic proxies

Practical limitations undermine theoretical assumptions: non-symmetric Jacobian in practice claimed to satisfy Proposition 1 'approximately' without formal justification; spectral gap assumption only empirically validated, not guaranteed

Initialization and hyperparameter dependence: geodesic optimization requires good initialization (SLERP); timestep τ selection appears dataset-dependent (τ ∈ [0.4T, 0.6T]) with no principled selection method; regularization variant (G + λI) dismissed based on undescribed 'preliminary experiments'
Unable to operate at t=0 (clean data space) due to metric degeneracy, limiting applicability in certain scenarios
Presentation issues: key theoretical details relegated to appendices; Figure 1 is conceptual without clear before/after visual comparisons; pullback metric interpretation could be more prominent

strengths: Well-designed Riemannian metric derived from score function Jacobian with clear mathematical foundation and elegant spectral characterization of tangent-normal separation
Training-free approach applicable to pre-trained models without requiring additional training or architectural modifications
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (2D synthetic, image, video) with diverse metrics (PPL, PDV, FID, RE, MSE, LPIPS) and systematic ablation studies
Consistent practical improvements demonstrated across interpolation quality, guidance-corrected generation, and distillation with clear visual evidence of detail preservation
Thorough experimental documentation with extensive appendices covering alternative constructions, computational costs, hyperparameter sensitivity, and additional datasets
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core insight that score Jacobian separates tangent/normal directions derives from prior work (Stanczuk et al. 2024, Ventura et al. 2025), with this paper's contribution being primarily application to metric definition

Incomplete theoretical justification: no rigorous proof that geodesics under this metric optimize perceptual interpolation quality; relies on intuitive but unproven assumptions about manifold-tangent paths

Questionable metric reliability: requires τ > 0 (spectral gap collapses at t=0), Jacobian is only approximately symmetric with undefined behavior requiring regularization (Appendix B), and when these approximations hold is not characterized
Computational overhead significantly higher than closed-form baselines (Table 6); iterative optimization per interpolation path limits scalability and practical deployment

Modest empirical improvements on guidance correction (Table 4): marginal FID gains over CFG++ with statistical significance unclear; benefit appears to be preventing distortion rather than quality enhancement
Hyperparameter sensitivity with unclear practical guidance: multiple hyperparameters (τ, λ, CG iterations) with non-obvious settings and critical dependence on τ without principled selection strategy

Limited experimental scope: primarily 512×512 images without high-resolution testing; no comparison with recent diffusion-based or flow-matching interpolation methods or other geometry-aware approaches
Gap between theory and practice: multiple approximations (symmetric Jacobian, regularization requirements) and their cumulative effects not quantified; unclear when metric quality degrades
